opus-5.5.text:
Well, I should say up front that I'm not a games industry person. My day job is language and machine learning, so take this as the view of an interested outsider rather than an expert.

The interesting thing is that for a long stretch the AAA industry measured itself against movies. You saw it in the vocabulary: "cinematic experiences," big-name actors doing motion capture, budgets that rival or exceed Hollywood blockbusters, cutscenes that are essentially short films. In some ways games converged on movies, especially in visual fidelity and linear storytelling.

But I think the fundamental distinction never went away, and maybe it has sharpened. A movie is an authored artifact. The director controls exactly what you see, in what order, and for how long. A game is a system. The designer sets up rules, a world, and affordances, and the experience emerges from the player's choices. The best games lean into that. The ones that just string together cutscenes with some shooting in between often feel like neither a great movie nor a great game.

Economically they've diverged too. Movies are mostly a one-time purchase of a ticket or a stream. Big games have shifted toward ongoing services, with live operations, seasons, and in-game economies. So the product isn't a finished work anymore; it's something that keeps evolving.

Where this connects to my world is interactivity and language. Historically, games could give you a rich physical world, but conversation with characters was very limited: dialogue trees with three or four canned options. Now, with large language models, there's at least the possibility of characters you can actually talk to, who respond sensibly to what you say. That pushes games even further away from the movie model, because the narrative becomes even less pre-scripted. Whether that makes for better storytelling is an open question. Authored stories have a coherence and craft that's hard to get from generation on the fly. But I think that tension between authored narrative and emergent interaction is really the heart of the movies-versus-games distinction, and AI is going to make it a lot more interesting.

r001.rationale: The response says AAA games converged on movies in visual fidelity and linear storytelling, and points to cinematic experiences, actors, large budgets, and cutscenes as signs of that convergence.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, it's an interesting question, and I should say up front that games aren't really my area—I'm a natural language processing person—but I've watched this from the outside with some interest, partly because of what it says about where interactive media and AI might intersect.

The classic distinction was that a movie is a fixed artifact. The director controls every frame, the pacing, what you look at, what you feel at minute forty-two. A game, in principle, hands some of that control to the player. But what's striking about the AAA industry over the last fifteen or twenty years is how much it has converged toward the movie model. You have these enormous productions—hundreds of people, budgets that rival or exceed Hollywood films—and a lot of that money goes into cinematic cutscenes, motion-captured performances, scripted set pieces. The player is often being guided down a fairly narrow corridor, and the "choice" is somewhat illusory. People sometimes joke that the big prestige games are movies with a bit of interactivity sprinkled on top.

So I'd actually say the distinction has gotten blurrier, not sharper, at the high end. Where it stays sharp is in the places where the interaction is genuinely generative—where the system responds to what you do in ways the designers didn't fully script. Simulation games, emergent sandbox games, and increasingly anything with procedural or AI-driven content.

And that's where my field comes in. The one thing games have never really been able to do is let you talk to the characters. Dialogue trees are the AAA solution, and they're fundamentally a branching movie script. Language models change that calculus. If a non-player character can actually understand and respond to what you say, you get something that is categorically not a movie—it's closer to improvisational theater, with all the messiness that implies. Whether the big studios embrace that, given how much they've invested in authorial control and polish, is an open question. My guess is it will come from smaller studios first, the way most interesting things do.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly says the distinction between movies and games has gotten “blurrier” as the AAA industry has developed.

astra-6.text:
I think the interesting distinction is that movies give you a story that somebody has already decided how to tell. You can be emotionally involved, but you don’t get to change what happens. Games give you some agency: you’re acting in a world, and that world responds to you.

As the AAA games industry has developed, it’s also become much more cinematic, with elaborate stories, actors, and very expensive production. And that creates a tension. If you’re essentially moving between scripted scenes, you have this wonderful-looking experience, but the range of things you can actually do may still be quite narrow.

To me, the exciting possibility is to make that interaction richer—to have characters that you can talk to and that respond meaningfully to what you say and do. That would allow games to develop in a direction where the experience depends much more on the player, rather than simply borrowing the storytelling techniques of movies.

r001.rationale: The response says AAA games have become much more cinematic, with elaborate stories, actors, and expensive production, conveying that their development has brought them closer to movies.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the distinction has become less clear in some ways. If you look at AAA games, an enormous amount of effort goes into the same things that matter in movies: visual realism, characters, storytelling, and production values. And you can end up with a game where you’re essentially watching a movie interspersed with opportunities to do something.

But the interesting difference is that a game can respond to you. You’re acting in a world, and your actions should have consequences. That creates a tension: the more tightly you script a compelling story, the more you constrain what the player can actually do. To me, the exciting possibility is to have richer characters and worlds that can respond dynamically, so that interaction becomes a central part of the experience.

r001.rationale: The response says the distinction between movies and games has “become less clear” as AAA games emphasize movie-like visuals, characters, storytelling, and production values.
